Consider the **orthonormal** set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an **orthonormal** basis of ${R}^{2}.$ What is the value of $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|?$

$$
U={[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]}
$$

examples.knowledge_point: Extending a Set to Form an Orthonormal Basis
examples.problem:
Consider the **orthonormal** set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $\mathbf x = [x_1,\,x_2,\,x_3]^T,$ extend the set so that it forms an **orthonormal** basis of $\mathbb{R}^3.$ 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065835/assets/969339570bc776ebf69a7f6e9cbff0377fa35842a913e68680d8bd2ed0a1decb.png)
examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of ${U}$ as $\mathbf{u}_1,\, \mathbf{u}_2.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^3,$ we need to find a third vector $\mathbf{x}$ such that $\| \mathbf{x} \|=1$ and

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065835/assets/e7034bdd15c1adc9aca80284bb2ab9b5a99ce5f33fa65f7b867c542158727b9d.png)

So, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\sqrt{2}\cdot {R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=\sqrt{6}\cdot {R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). This means $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get $x_2=-x_3,$ and from the first equation, we obtain $x_1=x_3.$

So, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14065835/assets/e690911497bbee717323b680e92c57a7ab9d6d9d78d6ed3440d2657cd5883c3d.png)

Setting $x_3=1,$ we obtain the vector

feedback.problem:
Consider the orthogonal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3},\,{x}_{4}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}.$ What is the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{4}}?$

$$
U={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2},\,{u}_{3}.$ To extend the given set to an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}$, we need to find a fourth vector $x$ such that

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{3}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}-{x}_{4}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}-2{x}_{4}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are three pivot columns ($1$st, $2$nd and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{4}$ is a free variable. From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=-{x}_{4}$ and ${x}_{3}=-2{x}_{4}$, respectively. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+(-{x}_{4})+(-2{x}_{4})+{x}_{4}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2{x}_{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{4} \\ -{x}_{4} \\ -2{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{4}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{4}=1,$ we obtain the vector 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}$ is

$$
{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{4}}=\frac{2}{1}=2.$
